content: Whole grain breakfast cereals, whole grain bakery products, and vitamin A-rich orange vegetables were identified as key dietary components. The diversity of food subgroups was lower in liberalized dietary models, where larger quantities of fewer subgroups were selected. Feasible food pattern solutions included four or five of the five main food groups, while liberalized models included only three groups. Model solutions also incorporated six or seven of the eight IYCF (Infant and Young Child Feeding) indicator food groups. For this age group, there were no gaps in target nutrients, so liberalized models were not necessary. Once nutrient targets were met, the Optifood software minimized protein intake, which was reflected in the results. Food patterns for this age group included more servings of staple foods, with the number of servings increasing across energy intake levels. Staples consisted primarily of whole grains, with small amounts of roots, tubers, and plantains included at higher energy levels. Added fats and oils were not selected in any food pattern. Fruits were included in all feasible food patterns, with servings increasing across energy levels. The high-energy solution reached the weekly maximum for fruit servings. Similarly, all food patterns included the maximum weekly servings of vegetables. For protein foods, the diversity of subgroups and the total number of servings decreased as energy intake levels increased. This was likely because higher energy levels met nutrient needs with larger quantities of less protein-dense foods, and because the Optifood software minimized protein once nutrient targets were achieved. Notably, this age group was the only one modeled where nuts and seeds were included in the solutions. Unlike breastfed infants, added fats and oils were included in all model solutions for non-breastfed children. Across the three model solutions, certain food subgroups were consistently selected at maximum levels, including whole grain breakfast cereals, dark green leafy vegetables, vitamin A-rich orange vegetables, immature peas/beans, soy foods, and liver. Other subgroups, such as whole grain bakery products, berries, and other vegetables, were selected at maximum levels in two energy scenarios. High-fat fruits were included only in the high-energy scenario. The food patterns demonstrated high diversity, including numerous vegetable and protein subgroups. All patterns included both animaland plant-based protein sources. The patterns also incorporated four or five of the five main food groups and six or seven of the eight IYCF indicator food groups. For starchy staples, five daily servings per week were included. The absence of nutrient gaps in the model solutions eliminated the need for liberalized models. Once nutrient targets were met, the software minimized protein intake, which was evident in the results. When food subgroups or groups were eliminated, macronutrient profiles for infants showed minimal changes. However, eliminating both fruits and vegetables led to higher protein intake and lower carbohydrate intake. Eliminating vegetables increased dairy and protein foods, likely to meet iron and mineral needs. Removing flesh foods (e.g., meat, liver, poultry, fish) increased dairy and plant-based protein foods. Staple foods remained at the minimum required servings in all scenarios. For older infants, eliminating whole grain staples reduced starchy staple foods to the minimum and increased fruit consumption. Removing vegetables increased dairy and starchy staples, particularly whole grains. Eliminating legumes, nuts, and seeds increased whole grain staples and animal-based protein foods. Removing liver and small fish increased other animal-based protein foods, while broader elimination of flesh foods increased dairy consumption. When unhealthy items like sweetened beverages or biscuits were included, protein intake decreased, and carbohydrate intake increased. Frequent inclusion of unhealthy items displaced nearly all other complementary foods and beverages. Substituting unhealthy items for whole grains created nutrient gaps, particularly for minerals, and required the selection of more nutrient-dense protein foods. Including fortified items like multiple micronutrient powders (MNPs) or small-quantity lipid-based nutrient supplements (SQ-LNS) led to shifts in food group contributions. For example, SQ-LNS displaced most vegetables, dairy, and protein foods. MNPs eliminated nearly all protein foods but retained dairy. These shifts reflect the nutrient-dense nature of fortified items, which meet micronutrient needs without contributing significant energy. In summary, the dietary models demonstrated the importance of diverse food groups, particularly whole grains, fruits, vegetables, and protein sources, in meeting nutrient needs. Eliminating key food groups or including unhealthy items significantly altered nutrient profiles, emphasizing the need for balanced and nutrient-dense diets for infants and young children.
